ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a relaxed, collegial videoconference style with mostly short-to-medium turns in the opening and Q&A, contrasted with long, structured presentation turns. Participants use frequent acknowledgments (“yeah,” “okay,” “great”), light small talk, and occasional joking before shifting abruptly into formal introductions and talks. Speech is highly spontaneous and disfluent: fillers such as “um,” repetitions, self-corrections, abandoned starts, and loosely formed questions are common, especially among non-native speakers. Overlap and interruptions are low; speakers generally wait, though brief backchanneling and quick interjections occur. Questions are usually prefaced with praise or hedging (“I have a quick question,” “maybe,” “I’m not sure”), then develop through multiple follow-ups. Disagreement is indirect and framed as uncertainty, alternative explanations, or open questions rather than confrontation. Responses tend to validate the question first, qualify limits of the evidence, and then reason aloud through possibilities.

Meeting style for this meeting (deferential_junior): A senior person leads and a more junior person is cautious, checks before offering ideas ('this might be a dumb question') and sometimes holds back something useful. A third person occasionally draws them out. The senior person is friendly but sometimes talks over them.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - This might be a dumb question, but is that normal for this kind of data?
  - No, it's fine, it's- well, it depends. Go ahead.
  - Sorry, I was going to say, in my group we usually-
Opening: Start with a person asking for a quick catch-up because they missed the last meeting.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Evaluating an AI math tutor used in middle-school classrooms and deciding what it should and should not do for students.

speakers.name: Dr. Mei Chen
speakers.background: A fourth-year PhD student in learning technologies who has spent three years building and evaluating NLP-assisted math-feedback systems. Her work uses held-out, anonymized student-work datasets to test error classification and hint quality, along with usability telemetry, privacy-preserving logging, and school-network performance testing. She has supported pilots in public-school settings and is attentive to making system limits visible to educators.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Chen treats the tutor as a fallible technical system whose behavior must be tested before classroom use. She focuses on whether error detection is accurate across varied student work, whether graduated hints reliably stop short of completing problems, whether latency is acceptable on school networks, and whether event logs can answer research questions without exposing student identities. She will lead validation of error-detection and hint behavior using held-out anonymized work, network latency testing, and pseudonymized logging design, while relying on education and psychology colleagues to define what counts as useful, safe classroom behavior.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Ms. Rosa Alvarez
speakers.background: A middle-school mathematics instructional coach with 16 years of experience as a Grade 6–8 teacher, department chair, and district curriculum facilitator. She has led implementation of digital math tools across multiple classrooms and uses lesson observations, teacher interviews, student-work review, and formative-assessment planning to study whether a tool fits real instructional routines. She is familiar with linear-equation misconceptions and the practical constraints of managing mixed-readiness classrooms.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Alvarez judges the tutor by its instructional fit rather than its technical novelty. She focuses on when students may use it, how teachers introduce and monitor it without losing instructional time, what off-task or workaround behavior looks like, and whether weekly summaries give teachers actionable evidence for next lessons. She will lead classroom-use routines, an observation protocol for teacher workload and off-task use, and requirements for teacher-facing formative-assessment summaries. She strongly favors keeping teachers in control of instruction, grading, and student support.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Arjun Patel
speakers.background: A school and developmental psychologist with 11 years of experience studying adolescent motivation, academic anxiety, self-regulated learning, and help-seeking during STEM instruction. He has designed brief classroom-friendly pre/post measures and mixed-methods studies combining student surveys, behavior coding, and teacher reports. In cross-disciplinary pilots, he coordinates timelines and decision logs while ensuring that behavioral indicators are interpreted cautiously rather than treated as simple proof of engagement.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Patel asks how the tutor changes students' emotional and motivational relationship to difficult mathematics. He is concerned that a hint can support persistence for one student but encourage passive dependence or disengagement for another. He will lead selection of brief, age-appropriate pre/post measures of math anxiety and motivation and develop a coding procedure for hint responses, including persistence, disengagement, and over-reliance. He will also help specify how observed distress or repeated disengagement should be routed to the teacher through the school's existing support process, rather than through automated intervention.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Hold a planning meeting with Dr. Chen (computer science), Ms. Alvarez (education), and Dr. Patel (psychology). The group must agree on coordinated next steps for the April 13 pilot and assign each task to the discipline best positioned to lead it, while allowing stated collaboration where needed. Dr. Chen should explain that computer science can validate error-detection and hint behavior using a held-out set of anonymized student work, run school-network latency tests, and implement privacy-preserving event logging with student identifiers removed or pseudonymized. Ms. Alvarez should explain that education can define classroom routines for when students may use the tutor, create an observation protocol for teacher workload and off-task use, and specify formative-assessment evidence teachers need from a weekly summary. Dr. Patel should explain that psychology can select brief age-appropriate pre/post measures of math anxiety and motivation and design a procedure for reviewing whether hints lead students to persist, disengage, or become over-reliant. The team should make three decisions: the tutor may give error-specific graduated hints but may not provide final answers or complete multi-step problems for students; teachers receive weekly class-level summaries rather than real-time student rankings; and any student distress or repeated disengagement observed during the pilot is referred to the teacher under the school’s existing support process. The meeting should establish dependencies and dates: Chen will provide a testable tutor build and logging specification by March 6; Alvarez will provide classroom routines, observation protocol, and teacher-summary requirements by March 13; Patel will provide measures and the hint-response coding guide by March 13; Chen will integrate the approved requirements by March 27; the full team will conduct a teacher walkthrough and network check during the week of March 30; and the team will review pilot data together after the first two weeks of use. Do not claim that consent procedures, district data approval, or the exact sample size have been finalized; these remain open items requiring school/district confirmation before student data collection.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Rosa Alvarez
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. Before we get into it, I missed the very end of our last conversation. Did anything change around the district data approval? I was hoping today we could get concrete about what this looks like in an actual Grade 7 class, especially the teacher routine while students are on the tutor, because April will come around very, very quickly.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arjun Patel
transcript.text: I don't think anything changed, Rosa. Consent procedures, district approval, and the final sample are still awaiting confirmation. For the classroom routine, I'd want a really simple teacher-facing route if there's repeated withdrawal or visible distress, through the school's existing support process, not something the tutor tries to manage on its own. What do your teachers already see as the line between normal productive struggle and a student who's really checking...

transcript.speaker: Ms. Rosa Alvarez
transcript.text: For most teachers, normal frustration still looks like engagement. They’re writing, trying a different step, maybe asking a peer or waiting to ask the teacher. The concern is when that stops—head down, repeated clicking with no change in written work, or just reopening hints. But I’d want the teacher to notice a pattern, not flag one rough problem.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: That distinction is helpful. So for the logs, I’d be cautious about treating repeated hints or a pause on its own as a disengagement signal. We could surface a small class-level pattern for the teacher, but not generate a student flag. Rosa, when students show incomplete work, just an answer or one partial line, how common is that in this unit? Our error detector is less, um, steady on those than on fully written steps.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Rosa Alvarez
transcript.text: Pretty common, especially early in the unit and with students who aren't confident writers in math. A partial line can mean they know what operation comes next, or it can just be a rushed entry, so I wouldn't want the tutor naming it as an error. It should ask for the next step or let the student say they're, they're not finished. Could it keep that distinction visible in the log?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: I think so. We can log it as something like “insufficient work to classify,” separate from a detected error, and have the tutor give a neutral prompt rather than a correction. I’d want to test that on the held-out work first, because incomplete entries are exactly where a confident-looking wrong label would be most harmful.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Rosa Alvarez
transcript.text: That wording matters a lot. If the weekly view separates "not enough work to classify" from actual error patterns, a teacher can decide whether to look at the notebook or confer with the student instead of assuming the system knows. Could the student-facing prompt be something like, "Show your next step when you’re ready," instead of pushing them to type a full explanation?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arjun Patel
transcript.text: Mm, that seems important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: We can make it exactly that, “Show your next step when you’re ready,” and record that the system didn’t classify the entry, not that the student made an error. I’d also keep the weekly view to counts and patterns, with the actual student work staying with the teacher, because the log can’t tell why a line is partial.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Rosa Alvarez
transcript.text: That’s the right boundary. For the March 20 plan, I need the weekly summary to show those categories clearly alongside class-level use, without turning it into a list of kids to chase. I can pull together the teacher routine, observation notes, and summary requirements by March 13, and then we should test the actual build with teachers in the week of March 30, not just review screenshots.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: That sounds workable. I can have the testable build and the logging specification ready by March 6, so the summary categories are in something teachers can react to before the March 30 session. I do need to check both schools' device and network setup before we promise the same, the same response time in a full class, though, especially with the logging on.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Rosa Alvarez
transcript.text: Please include the actual student log-in and first problem in that check, not just a speed test. If the response drags, the teacher ends up filling the dead time, and then the routine falls apart. Do we know yet whether the schools can give the participating teachers protected time for that walkthrough and for looking at the weekly summary?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arjun Patel
transcript.text: That protected time also affects whether any student measures are feasible. I can keep the pre/post very brief, but I need to check with both schools what class time is actually available and whether the district is comfortable with the wording. We shouldn't add it just because the logs exist. And the walkthrough could test the teacher routine for noticing patterns without making the weekly summary feel like another, another surveillance task.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Rosa Alvarez
transcript.text: Exactly. If a teacher has to decode a dashboard during a passing period, it won't get used. I'd rather test whether they can glance at one short class pattern, check a couple of notebooks or have a quick conference, and use that to shape the next day's warm-up. That's about the limit of what feels...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: That gives us a pretty concrete test. Can a teacher use one class-level pattern to choose a warm-up without having to interpret individual log trails? Once Rosa’s summary requirements and Arjun’s measures are settled, I can fold those into the build by March 27, so the March 30 walkthrough is using the same reporting setup we’d take into the April 13...

transcript.speaker: Ms. Rosa Alvarez
transcript.text: For that walkthrough, I want teachers to actually use the summary to pick a warm-up from a realistic set of student work, and then tell us what they would do next. Otherwise we might prove the report displays correctly without- without learning whether it helps them teach a mixed group.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, I’d like to see that.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arjun Patel
transcript.text: I’d add one small piece to that exercise. After teachers choose the warm-up, ask what evidence they’d need before concluding a pattern reflects disengagement rather than, um, students using hints strategically. The same hint count can mean pretty different things, so I think the walkthrough should make that ambiguity visible instead of asking the summary to settle it.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Rosa Alvarez
transcript.text: That’s exactly the question I’d put in front of them. I’d also ask what they’d check first, the student’s paper, a quick conversation, maybe what was happening in the room, because the log should be a reason to look, not evidence by itself. And if they’d need five different screens to- if that’s what the answer is, then we’ve made it too complicated.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: I can make the summary deliberately thin, just one or two class patterns, with a plain note that they're prompts to check work or talk to students, not conclusions. For the walkthrough, could we also watch whether teachers understand the "insufficient work to classify" category without us explaining it? If that label gets read as a deficit, we should change it before April.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Rosa Alvarez
transcript.text: Let’s test that cold, with no legend beyond whatever would actually be on the page. “Insufficient work to classify” may be accurate, but I can imagine a teacher reading it as, you know, this child didn’t do enough. Maybe “entry not yet classifiable” lands differently? We should see what they say before we decide.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arjun Patel
transcript.text: Hm, worth testing cold.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: I can put two or three candidate labels into the March 30 version and keep the underlying event separate from whatever wording teachers see. And the network check should include that exact summary page too, not just tutor responses. I was thinking the thin report- if it takes too long to load, it still won’t be usable.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Rosa Alvarez
transcript.text: And I want the network check to happen with a whole-class kind of load, if the schools will allow it, not one laptop in an empty room. A slow summary page on Friday afternoon is one thing, but a slow first login with thirty seventh-graders is where the teacher routine really...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: I’ll check whether each school can give us a realistic concurrent-login test, including the first problem submission, hint delivery, and the summary page. If they can’t, I don’t think we should pretend a single-device result tells us much. I’ll also need their filtering and device details before I can say what telemetry will actually work.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Rosa Alvarez
transcript.text: While you’re getting those details, I need to know what time the teachers can actually give us that week. A realistic load test is useful, but the walkthrough also needs enough protected time for them to try the routine and the summary without rushing out to pick up a class. I’ll check with the schools rather than assume that’s...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arjun Patel
transcript.text: That makes sense. Once Rosa knows what protected time is available, I can check whether a genuinely brief pre/post fits there without displacing instruction. If it doesn't, I'd rather omit it than rush students through it. And we should keep all of that contingent on the district approval and consent decision.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Rosa Alvarez
transcript.text: I’ll get the protected-time answer from both schools, and I’ll make the March 30 walkthrough contingent on actually having enough time to run the routine, the whole-class check, and that warm-up exercise. If they can’t give us that, we need to say so plainly in the March 20 plan rather than quietly, quietly adding work to teachers’ plates.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: Okay, I think we’re at time. Thanks, everyone—I'll see you at the next check-in.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Rosa Alvarez
transcript.text: All right, take care, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arjun Patel
transcript.text: Thank you, everyone. Goodbye.
